data.title: 'She's living the dream': My stepmother said I can buy my childhood home for $850,000. Is she taking advantage of me?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'My late father bought our house for $250,000 in the 1990s'

"She said if my dad wanted me to have it, he should have arranged that before he died." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

My late father bought our house for $250,000 in the 1990s. By the time he died, it was worth about $850,000, mostly because it's spacious and in a good neighborhood. He left it to my stepmother, whom he married a few years after my mom died. She is now 74. They were together for 18 years. She took care of him through the whole illness, which I don't take lightly.

Dad told me more than once that the house would be mine someday. My stepmother now wants to sell and move somewhere smaller. She's living the dream in Miami. I offered $700,000. That's $200,000 under market, but I thought it was fair, given that she would skip agent fees and it would be a quick, clean sale. I'd have to stretch to do it, but I could manage.

She was really offended, and she told me as much. She said she's paid the property taxes and the repairs for years (she put a new roof on in 2021). She also said she spent a big chunk of her own savings on my father's care and that the house is basically her retirement plan, and that she can't just hand me $200,000 because I'm sentimental.

Don't miss: My wife says we can't afford to retire. I vetoed her $8,000 trip to Italy. We're in our 60s and have $4 million. Do I keep working?

The $200,000 discount

That's a fair point, and I told her so. What I can't get past is that a few years ago she gave her daughter $200,000 toward a house, and that is how (and why) I came up with the $200,000 haircut on my father's home. I brought that up, and she said things were different then, and pointed out that I have a good job and can buy my own place.

She said if my dad wanted me to have it, he should have arranged that before he died. As my girlfriend at the time said, "Yes, she really went there." That comment really stung. He trusted her with everything, and it feels like his wishes just evaporated. She says she honored him by caring for him and that I'm discounting everything she sacrificed.

I could, of course, walk away and buy somewhere else. I've even looked at a couple of listings. But it wouldn't be the same, and I'd always feel like the house slipped away from our family. I know that my stepsister's place has a sauna in the basement, and I'd bet anything that my stepmother helped pay for that too. Not that I'm keeping score. (OK, I know I am a little.)

Am I being unreasonable?

The Stepson

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: My wife never went back to work after raising our kids. Do I have to share my retirement savings 50/50?

You can't force someone to sell you a house that never legally belonged to you.

Dear Stepson,

Don't allow steam from your stepsister's sauna to cloud your vision. You can grieve the loss of your childhood home without assigning blame.

What's more, you can't force someone to sell you a house that never belonged to you in the first place. Your childhood home, legally and morally, belonged to your father. Even though you grew up there, that doesn't give you the right to a life estate or a $200,000 discount on the purchase price because your stepmother gave her daughter $200,000 toward the down payment on her own home. What's more, selling a house to a family member below fair market value can create a gift of equity equal to the price difference, which the IRS may treat as a taxable gift.

Your late father made a promise that he did not keep, could not keep or decided not to keep. That was his responsibility. It's not your stepmother's job to make good on your father's promises. Whether he made a will leaving her the house or whether she inherited the house through state intestate laws, the end result is the same: She legally owns the house, and she has the right to live there or sell it to whomever she wants.

It is your belief that your father's wishes "evaporated." But wishes, promises and/or intentions evolve, and perhaps he realized that he wanted to take care of his wife of nearly two decades, and die with the knowledge that she would always have a roof over her head. It would have been better to have discussed those plans with you rather than leaving you in a kind of limbo, wondering if he truly wanted to leave his estate to his wife. Chances are, he did.

That does not mean this is an easy or pleasant situation for you. You have an emotional attachment to this property, and you regard your stepmother as an interloper, inheriting a property where your own mother probably once lived. It's a tough break for you and your siblings, if you have any. You made your stepmother an offer and she declined. She may be thinking about her own retirement and financial future.

Don't miss: 'I don't feel sorry for myself': I'm 64 and will be renting for the rest of my life. Is that so bad?

Passing judgment

Two decades is a long time to spend with someone. She met your father when she was in her 50s, and she's now rightly concerned about medical costs, if she needs nursing home care, especially if she does not have long-term care insurance, or any other kind of life insurance. This house may be the only asset she has, and downsizing will give her a cushion as she heads towards her 80th birthday in six years. That's quite a reality check.

I'm heartened that you realize that taking care of your father was no small deal for your stepmother. Who will take care of her if she sells you this house for $650,000 and runs out of money? Will you drive her to hospital appointments and spend hours a day with her, making sure that she takes her medication and pays her bills, and has enough to eat? That might sound dramatic, but getting older often comes with health complications.

One could argue that you both "went there." She "went there" by telling you your father wanted her to have his house. You "went there" by using emotional leverage, whether or not you believe it in your heart to be valid, to persuade her to sell this house to you on the cheap. By doing so, you are, whether you realize it or not, also passing judgment on her marriage of 18 years to a man she probably loved very much. You both spoke plainly. That's OK. Just know it's 50/50.

If you want this house, put in an offer when it is listed for sale. If she does get more than one offer and, say, one party offers $50,000 more, she may still decide to sell you the house (and maybe not even mention that she is selling it to you at less than the other offer). Remember, if she gets $950,000 rather than $850,000 - a real possibility if it's a cash buyer and it's a sought-after neighborhood - she would have been giving you a $300,000 discount if she agreed to your proposal.

All is fair in love, second marriages, legal beneficiaries and real estate. Just don't overstretch yourself financially for the sake of nostalgia.

Related: 'People in the U.S. need to wake up': As a mortgage loan officer, I rejected applications from wealthy couples. Here's why.

data.title: AI fever ignites a boom in thematic ETFs as fund managers hunt for their next big hit
data.description:
By Christine Idzelis

It's been a rocky October for the AI trade, putting a dent in big gains so far this year

Robotics ETFs are increasingly coming to the stock market, with AI being a dominant investing theme in 2026.

The runaway success of the artificial-intelligence trade has left investors hungry for the next big market theme. Wall Street fund managers are happily obliging with a flurry of new targeted products, helping investors invest in everything from the rise of robotics to the incipient space economy.

Thematic ETFs are booming in 2026, as asset managers have launched new products at a breakneck pace. The popularity of funds like the Roundhill Memory ETF DRAM, which invests in memory stocks as a subsector of technology and quickly gained traction because they're an important part of the AI trade, has inspired something of a gold rush in the space, as fund companies cast about for the next big hit.

Niche subdivisions of the AI theme have proved particularly popular, as fund managers have launched products tied to everything from AI lab ecosystems to shares of optical companies expected to benefit from the ongoing AI investment boom. Cybersecurity, robotics and defense have been other popular themes.

"AI is the dominant theme," said Bryan Armour, director of ETF and semiliquid fund research at Morningstar, in a phone interview. "What we're seeing in 2026 is product development that refines some of those exposures," he said, from AI Labs to robotics including humanoids.

So far, 73 thematic ETFs have launched this year in the U.S., an 87% increase from the 39 launches seen in 2025, according to data from Morningstar. But the boom in new products is also dredging up some uncomfortable memories: The previous peak for thematic ETF launches arrived in 2021, as the COVID-era market mania was reaching its crescendo. 

 
Thematic ETF launches are surging in 2026 
Year                                          Launches 
2020                                          49 
2021                                          90 
2022                                          59 
2023                                          40 
2024                                          25 
2025                                          39 
2026                                          73 
Source: Morningstar data as of Oct. 19, 2026

While broad index funds like the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF SPY continue to dominate the league tables of products with the most assets under management, the growth in the thematic space suggests investors are increasingly fixating on a more specific opportunity set.

Over the past couple of years, AI has become more influential as an economic force. Economists now say aggressive investment in new data centers is largely responsible for a pickup in the pace of GDP growth.

"This is one of the biggest themes in a generation," said Jay Jacobs, U.S. head of equity ETFs at BlackRock, in a phone interview. "If you look at what's driving the markets, AI is up there with GDP growth and interest rates as one of the biggest factors."

BlackRock listed on Wednesday the iShares Future Robotics and Related Technologies Active ETF RBTX, which actively invests in stocks in categories such as humanoids, industrial automatization, autonomous vehicles, and space and defense, according to Jacobs.

"This is really looking out at what the next major development could look like in the artificial-intelligence space," he said. "The next phase is really AI entering the physical world."

It's hardly the first robotics-focused product to launch this year. Indeed, it has been a particularly popular theme, according to Aniket Ullal, head of ETF research and analytics at CFRA Research. A handful of products have launched in recent months, including the Tuttle-Rareview Humanoid Robotics ETF HOID, which began trading earlier this month.

"People are trying to disaggregate the AI theme," Ullal told MarketWatch by phone.

AI labs, space, cybersecurity

A bunch of AI-lab ETFs recently arrived to the market, including one centered around OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, which had helped popularize artificial intelligence after it was introduced to the public in late 2022.

Harbor Capital Advisors launched the OpenAI Lab Ecosystem ETF OAIW in August, along with the Anthropic AI Lab Ecosystem ETF ANTW, Meta AI Lab Ecosystem ETF MTAW, the Google DeepMind AI Lab Ecosystem ETF DEPW and SpaceXAI Lab Ecosystem ETF XAIW.

"The ecosystem is built around these frontier-model developers," said Armour. "They're like company-specific AI labs," with the ETFs holding shares of their partners or backers, he said.

As AI is maturing, many investors want to trade more precisely around the winners and losers as they shake out, according to Matthew Tuttle, CEO of Tuttle Capital Management.

For example, he pointed to the Roundhill Memory ETF, which launched in early April, as "a perfect product at the perfect time," during a phone interview with MarketWatch. The fund was the first ETF to focus on high-bandwidth memory stocks, providing exposure to the "biggest of the bottleneck trades" in AI, including shares of South Korean companies that U.S. investors couldn't easily buy at the time, he said. "Now what you're seeing, everyone is trying to come up with the next DRAM," said Tuttle, referring to the ETF's ticker.

Since then, he has launched other products offering exposure to the ongoing data-center buildout. In May, his firm launched the Tuttle Capital Pure Play Photonics ETF FOTO, which provides exposure to stocks involved in using laser light in optical fiber instead of copper wire for AI data centers. That same month saw the listing of the Corgi Lithography & Semiconductor Photonics ETF EUV, which Morningstar categorizes under the AI and Big Data theme.

Corgi has launched a flurry of ETF products this year, including a number of thematic funds, like the Corgi Robots & Humanoids ETF CBOT, Corgi Space & Satellite Communications ETF DIPR, Corgi Data & Surveillance ETF EYES, and Corgi AI Cybersecurity ETF XA, according to Morningstar data. Space, another popular theme, has been supercharged by the IPO of Elon Musk's SpaceX in June.

Cybersecurity has also been a big theme, as frontier AI models have seen their capabilities quickly advance. A few high-profile incidents where autonomous AI agents broke out of their sandboxes and infiltrated third-party systems have helped to underscore its importance.

The First Trust Nasdaq Cybersecurity ETF CIBR, which launched in 2015, is currently the biggest cybersecurity product in ETF land. It had $17 billion under management at the end of September, according to Morningstar data.

The AI trade's volatile October

It's been a rocky October for the AI trade as investors question the return on investment from companies doing a heavy amount of spending and borrowing relating to AI to support the buildout of the technology's infrastructure. Still, AI-related stocks have broadly seen big 2026 gains.

Among ETFs that invest in the broad theme, the iShares A. I. Innovation and Tech Active ETF BAI is up more than 21% in 2026 despite tumbling more than 14% this month through Friday. Similarly, the Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF AIQ has jumped more than 22% so far this year, although the fund had a much smaller October loss, of more than 4% through Friday, according to FactSet data.

AI is attracting heightened focus lately, after SpaceX (SPCX) reported third-quarter earnings on Oct. 20, and Facebook parent Meta Platforms (META) and Tesla (TSLA) each released quarterly results the following day. Next week brings highly anticipated results from other Big Tech companies involved in AI, including Google parent Alphabet (GOOGL) (GOOG).

With investors now getting access to many different funds with more precise exposures to AI, it's important to remember amid excitement over the transformative technology that "price matters" when identifying investing opportunities in the stock market, Armour cautioned.

"There's so much projection in valuing AI companies," he said, "that it makes it really hard to know whether you're still coming in before the full wave or if you're buying in on the crest."

Bull market for stocks

That S&P 500's strong run in 2026 and in each of the past three years appears to have set the stage for this year's jump in thematic ETFs, as investors sift through ways to sharpen their investing approach in the current bull market for U.S. stocks. The previous thematic ETF boom in 2021 - which Armour said was fueled in part by strategies around environmental, social and governance criteria known as ESG that included clean energy - also coincided with a strong bull market.

In 2021, the S&P 500 SPX booked its third consecutive year of double-digit percentage gains, before slumping 19.4% in 2022 to book its worst performance since 2008, according to FactSet data. The pace of thematic ETF launches fell off significantly in 2022.

AI has been a significant tailwind for the market this year, despite some concern over higher financing costs following a jump in bond yields and as many investors expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates again by year's end. The Fed had been raising rates aggressively in 2022, the year the U.S. stock market slumped, in an effort to battle soaring inflation.

Today, inflation remains elevated, albeit well below levels seen in 2022, prompting the Fed to hike its policy rate in September. The S&P 500 has climbed 11.4% this year through Friday, ending 2.5% below its record closing high booked Oct. 6, according to Dow Jones Market Data.

"When the stock market is particularly strong, then thematic funds tend to follow," said Armour. "When everything seems to be working, it's a lot easier to take on risk."

-Christine Idzelis

data.title: Moderna's cancer vaccine is 'likely' to get approved. Skeptics question if it will be the best option.
data.description:
By Jaimy Lee

The first Phase 3 data for a custom cancer vaccine has raised questions about whether the potential new treatment is needed

Moderna's stock was down slightly Friday, after plunging 17.6% on Thursday.

Moderna and Merck proved their custom cancer vaccine cut the risk of melanoma returning for longer than the cancer drug Keytruda, but it may take several years to understand if a therapeutic vaccine is better at beating the disease than immunotherapies.

The companies on Thursday released the highly anticipated Phase 3 data for intismeran, showing that a combination of the experimental vaccine and Merck's immunotherapy Keytruda reduced the risk of the cancer returning or the patient passing away by 42% after about two years compared to patients only taking Keytruda.

Though a seemingly striking outcome, the vaccine wasn't as efficacious as some investors had hoped. But the real test of intismeran will be how well the vaccine keeps cancer at bay over time. If it's successful, the custom treatment could radically change how certain patients with cancer are treated.

For now, however, the reaction to the data has been mixed. The study's results were unexpectedly released two days early as a result of a broken embargo, sending down the shares of both companies. Moderna's stock (MRNA) plummeted by as much as 25% on Thursday afternoon to close 17.6% lower. Merck's shares (MRK) closed 1.7% lower.

On Friday, Moderna's stock slipped 1.3%, as did Merck's shares.

Analysts speculated that the haphazard way that the Phase 3 results came out may have rattled investors. Some investors are also asking whether a brand-new technology like intismeran is as game-changing as it's promised to be, especially when compared to neoadjuvant immunotherapy, which is the practice of giving Keytruda and other immunotherapies to patients before they go through surgery to have their tumors removed.

"While approval seems likely, commercial success is far less certain," RBC Capital Markets analyst Trung Huynh told investors on Thursday. "The data raises fundamental questions about [intismeran's] value proposition relative to standards of care, particularly neoadjuvant immunotherapy, which produces similar efficacy at potentially much less cost."

Keytruda is often given to patients after surgery to prevent the return of their cancer, but sometimes it's administered to patients in advance of surgery to shrink the tumor.

A study published in 2023 found that giving Keytruda to patients with melanoma before surgery significantly extended how long they lived until the cancer came back or spread, or until the patient died, compared to those who received it after surgery. A Phase 3 trial of Yervoy and Opdivo, both of which are immunotherapies owned by Bristol Myers Squibb (BMY), had a similar outcome when given to patients with late-stage melanoma before surgery.

Both studies, however, were done in patients with clinically detectable Stage 3 cancer. That's how the doctors knew to administer the treatment before surgery. But the patients enrolled in the intismeran trial didn't know what stage of cancer they had until after they had surgery, according to Daniel Olson, an oncologist in the UChicago Medicine hospital system, which is one of the sites for other intismeran studies.

"People are saying, 'What's the value of an mRNA vaccine if you can just give [Keytruda] neoadjuvantly?'" he said. "Well, these patients, you can't."

Other analysts also questioned whether comparing studies with different patient populations is fair game.

"While we're not sure this is the right comparison, we see signs [intismeran and Keytruda] have a more durable effect," Jefferies analysts wrote in a note on Friday.

That's the big hope for intismeran, which is a therapeutic vaccine. Experts believe that the protective qualities that we associate with vaccines will work in cancer, hopefully creating lasting stretches of time before cancer comes back than what the currently available drugs can offer.

Intismeran works by training a patient's immune system to respond to the neoantigens in their tumor and then attack any residual cancer cells, according to Jane Healy, Merck's head of oncology early clinical development who ran the Phase 1 study for intismeran.

She believes that's why there was no difference between the patients who got the vaccine and those who got Keytruda in the first six months of the Phase 3 study. It takes time for the immune system to be trained, and for Healy, that means the benefits of a therapeutic vaccine will come later.

"It lends to the durability that [Keytruda] is going in and activating the immune system," she said in an interview. "But [intismeran] is training the immune system in what to recognize."

In the Phase 2 study for the vaccine, the hazard ratio - an important metric for understanding how well a new treatment performs compared to another drug or placebo - was 0.56 after about two years. But the most up-to-date data shows that the hazard ratio didn't degrade much over time, which commonly happens after experimental therapies move from smaller Phase 2 trials into larger Phase 3 studies. It was 0.51 after five years.

"The longer-term data from the Phase 2 - the five years - showing durable responses in these patients out to five years makes me hopeful that this new class of therapies is capable of this durable benefit," Healy said, later adding: "I'm hopeful that we're going to finally see that long-term benefit of vaccines that we get in infectious disease playing out in the oncology setting."

-Jaimy Lee

data.title: My husband wants to sell our $1.5 million home and invest the proceeds. But this is where we raised our kids - and I can't bear to leave.
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'He wants to buy something for $600,000 now that we are empty-nesters'

"We have another $1.8 million in retirement accounts and savings, plus Social Security." (Photo subjects are models.)

Dear Quentin,

I'm 67, my husband is 69, and we've been married 38 years. We've lived in the same four-bedroom colonial for 32 of those years. It's paid off and worth $1.5 million. We have another $1.8 million in retirement accounts and savings, plus Social Security and a small pension from his old job. No debt, and our kids are on their own.

So this isn't a money problem, but we can't talk about retirement anymore without it turning into a fight. He wants to buy something for $600,000 now that we are empty-nesters, and invest the rest. He has a spreadsheet. I've seen it open on the laptop at the kitchen table at 11 p.m., with property taxes, insurance and the lawn guy all in little columns.

He says we're heating rooms nobody uses, and he's right that nobody has slept in the fourth bedroom since our youngest left 12 years ago. It holds a treadmill (of course) and about nine boxes of Christmas decorations. He's also right that the place is a money pit. The roof has maybe three years left and the furnace sounds like it's clearing its throat every morning.

Last spring, we dropped $18,000 on a sewer line. Every time something breaks, Ron looks at me across the room like the case is closed. But the pantry door has pencil marks on it, one for every kid every year, with the dates in my handwriting. We brought both babies home to this house. He calls it sentimental clutter. I thought that was mean.

He slipped on the back steps last winter, and we both pretended it didn't scare us, but he could have just as easily slipped on another stairwell. All three kids live within an hour away. We host Thanksgiving every year, 14 people if everyone shows up, and the grandkids spend half of it out in the yard. Our daughter said she'd be sad if we sold.

I worry a small kitchen means the end of Thanksgiving, and that the grandkids will come less often if there's no yard. Ron says I'm inventing reasons because I'm scared of change. Maybe I am. But I don't want to be 75 and regret that we gave it up too soon. How do we decide whether staying is worth what it costs? Is it foolish to keep a house this big?

A Sentimental 67-Year-Old Homeowner

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: 'I am a pretty cautious person': My financial adviser wants me to invest $350,000 in a UAE data center. Is this risky?

I agree with your husband. I agree with you. Honestly, it's a tough call.

Dear Sentimental,

Take the pantry door with you when you go.

Joking aside, I think that's an idea worth exploring. Take whatever has sentimental value to your new home. If you live in a large, drafty house that costs money to heat, costs you thousands of dollars a year in property taxes and insurance, and you're only using a small number of rooms, it may no longer make financial sense to stay. But plenty of people live in the house where they raised their family because they love the house, the garden, and the feeling they get when they close the front door behind them. That's worth a lot.

It's as much a "money problem" as it is an everything-else problem. You have Social Security, which I'll assume is $4,000 a month between the two of you. If you follow the 4% rule and withdraw from your $1.8 million in savings in the first year, that would give you $72,000 before taxes. Whether your savings could endure that level of withdrawals over the rest of your lives depends on how much you spend, how you invest your nest egg, what happens in the stock market, how much you get in Social Security, and your husband's pension.

Your retirement fund could last until you're in your 90s, or for another 30 years (to be gloriously optimistic). An $80,000 income from $1.8 million equates to a 4.44% withdrawal rate in the first year, while an initial 4% withdrawal, adjusted for inflation in subsequent years, would give you $72,000 in the first year. You know your own lifestyle best, but this should give you a pretty good idea if you will need to downsize later. If you sold your house for $1.5 million and bought another for half the price, that would be a nice profit. You can afford to stay. You have choices.

There's plenty of room for discussion between his computer spreadsheet and your very real love for this place you call home. For starters, a lot of thought and time probably went into that spreadsheet. It may be his way of trying to make the next stage of your lives more secure. If you ended up with $2.7 million in investable assets after selling your home and buying another, a 4% initial withdrawal would - or could - give you an income of $108,000 a year before taxes. Would that difference affect how you want to live in retirement?

Related: My wife says we can't afford to retire, yet she wants to take an $8,000 trip to Italy. We have $4 million. Do I keep working?

A trial move

Moving makes more sense if you believe it would be expensive or impractical to future-proof your current home, with bedrooms and a decent bathroom on the ground floor. The costs of maintaining the house and your ability to live there safely as you age all matter. I agree with both of you that $18,000 for a sewer line is a lot of money, and that money could have been spent on a golf-club membership or several trips to Europe or South America. I agree with your husband. I agree with you. Honestly, it's a tough call.

What's the point of moving if one of you is unhappy? It's hard to imagine handing your home over to another couple or family and settling into a smaller space. If you talk to anyone who has lived in several properties throughout their life, they will probably have one home they still think about fondly. But it's "our" belongings - clothing, artwork, knickknacks, and all the stuff we accumulate (and get rid of as the years progress) - that create and, yes, recreate that familiar space that feels like home.

Explore your options with the help of a financial adviser, a couples therapist, or both. The former can help you compare the costs of staying versus going, while the latter can help you see each other's viewpoints. Once you have more clarity, an open discussion with your children could also help - not to get their approval, but to get their perspective. They know your family dynamics well and may have ideas. The starting point is that there is no "he's right and I'm wrong" or "I'm wrong and he's actually right." You both have valid points.

Rather than renting out your home or having strangers live among your belongings, why not spend some time in a rental property that could substitute as a long-term home. Visit open houses and imagine your life outside of this house, including during Thanksgiving and visits from your grandkids. It wouldn't hurt to have a survey done on your home to see how much you might have to pay for upgrades. You and your husband are not on opposing sides. You're on the same side. Just because he wants to downsize does not mean that he doesn't love the memories, too.

data.description:
BULL Investors Have Opportunity to Lead Webull Corporation Securities Fraud Lawsuit Filed by The Rosen Law Firm

BULL Investors Have Opportunity to Lead Webull Corporation Securities Fraud Lawsuit Filed by The Rosen Law Firm

data.title: BioInvent's BI-1808 and KEYTRUDA(R) Induce Durable Responses in Heavily Pretreated Platinum-Resistant Ovarian Cancer
data.description:
LUND, SE / ACCESS Newswire / October 24, 2026 / BioInvent International AB ("BioInvent") (Nasdaq Stockholm: BINV), a leader in the discovery of novel immune-modulatory antibodies, today announced updated data from Part B of its ongoing clinical study of BI-1808, a first-in-class anti-TNFR2 antibody, combined with MSD's (Merck & Co., Inc., Rahway, NJ, USA) anti-PD-1 therapy KEYTRUDA® (pembrolizumab) in patients with advanced platinum-resistant recurrent ovarian cancer (PRROC) and a median of four prior lines of therapy.

The data are presented today in poster #2009P (12:00-12:45 CEST) at the ESMO Congress 2026 in Madrid. They update the 25-patient analysis reported at ASCO 2026, the ESMO abstract published on October 19 and now include 34 evaluable patients (cutoff September 14, 2026).

Checkpoint inhibitors alone have limited activity in PRROC because CD8+ T cells poorly infiltrate the tumor microenvironment, where immunosuppressive TNFR2-expressing cells such as regulatory T cells (Tregs) and tumor-associated myeloid cells are enriched and further suppress antitumor T-cell activity. BI-1808 is a ligand-blocking, FcγR-engaging TNFR2 antibody designed to deplete these Tregs and remodel the myeloid compartment, promoting activation, expansion and infiltration of anti-tumoral CD8+ T cells.

"Patients with platinum-resistant ovarian cancer have few therapeutic options, and checkpoint inhibitors alone have done little to change that," said Martin Welschof, Chief Executive Officer at BioInvent. "With Part B complete, a 24% response rate and durable disease control in heavily pretreated patients suggest that targeting TNFR2 can add significant activity when combined with immune checkpoint inhibition. Our next step will be to evaluate BI-1808 as an add-on to the newly established pembrolizumab and paclitaxel backbone in a randomized Part C."

Durable responses in heavily pretreated patients
The 34 evaluable patients (of 40 planned) had a median age of 62 years and had received a median of four prior lines of therapy; 88% had received three or more, and all had received platinum. Histology was high-grade serous adenocarcinoma (HGSA) in 59% and clear cell in 41%, and 24% had liver involvement at screening. They were treated with BI-1808 1000 mg plus pembrolizumab 200 mg every three weeks for up to two years.

  • Responses were seen in both HGSA and clear cell ovarian cancer, including in patients with active liver metastases.
  • In some patients, tumors grew before shrinking. This may reflect pseudoprogression (an apparent increase in size caused by immune cells entering the tumor) or a delay in CD8+ T-cell expansion, an observation previously made in preclinical models (ASCO#2605 poster).
  • Most cases of progressive disease were not confirmed on a follow-up scan. These patients left the study with unconfirmed progressive disease under iRECIST, which explains the difference between PFS and iPFS.

What is iRECIST? iRECIST is an adaptation of the standard RECIST criteria for immunotherapies. It requires confirmation of progression before treatment is stopped, so it can capture responses that appear after initial apparent tumor growth. Median PFS by iRECIST may therefore be longer than by RECIST.

In KEYNOTE-100, pembrolizumab alone produced an objective response rate of 8% and a disease control rate of 37%. Median progression-free survival was 2.1 months by RECIST 1.1, and no iRECIST-based figure was reported.

Well tolerated, with fewer than 5% treatment-related discontinuations

  • 81 patients with solid tumors have received BI-1808 plus pembrolizumab to date
  • Immune-related adverse events were manageable, and the rate of Grade 3 or higher adverse events was low
  • Treatment-related discontinuations in the combination arm occurred in 4 patients (fewer than 5%)

Immune data consistent with the mechanism of BI-1808

  • Reduced Tregs in the blood of ovarian cancer patients, and a shift in the CD8+ T-cell over Treg ratio in tumor biopsies
  • Induction of IL-12 and CXCL10, cytokines associated with myeloid reprogramming, proinflammatory activation, and effector T cell recruitment
  • Induction of CCL19 and CXCL13, chemokines associated with tertiary lymphoid structure (TLS) formation
  • Proinflammatory myeloid and TLS-stimulating cytokines were strongly potentiated when BI-1808 was combined with pembrolizumab 2

Next step: adding BI-1808 to pembrolizumab and paclitaxel
The KEYNOTE-B96 study 3 recently added an immunotherapy option to the standard weekly paclitaxel ± bevacizumab regimen in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer, improving median PFS (8.3 vs 7.2 months) and overall survival (17.7 vs 14.0 months) versus chemotherapy alone. This creates a backbone on which to test additional mechanisms.

In a mouse model of ovarian cancer (ID8), the combination of a BI-1808 surrogate antibody, paclitaxel and anti-PD-1 improved survival, with increases in serum cytokines indicating myeloid reprogramming and TLS formation.

Part C of the study will randomize 20 patients to each of three arms: BI-1808 1000 mg, BI-1808 500 mg, or control, each with pembrolizumab and weekly paclitaxel +/- bevacizumab. Part C is expected to start in Q1 2027, with first data in H2 2027, subject to enrollment.

Poster details
Title: From Modest to Meaningful: Targeting TNFR2 with BI-1808 to Unlock Checkpoint Inhibitor Efficacy in Platinum-Resistant Recurrent Ovarian Cancer (PRROC)
Poster number: 2009P | Session: Investigational immunotherapy
Date and time: October 24, 12:00-12:45 CEST
First author: Rebecca Kristeleit, Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust, United Kingdom

The poster will be available on the publications tab of the BioInvent website: https://www.bioinvent.com/en/our-science/scientific-publications

About the trial
The BI-1808 study (NCT04752826, KEYNOTE-D20) is an ongoing open-label Phase 1/2a study evaluating BI-1808 as a single agent (Part A), in combination with pembrolizumab (Part B) and in combination with pembrolizumab and paclitaxel ± bevacizumab (Part C). Patients were enrolled at 14 study locations in Europe and the United States.

Clinical trial collaboration and supply agreement
KEYTRUDA® is a registered trademark of Merck Sharp & Dohme LLC, a subsidiary of Merck & Co., Inc., Rahway, NJ, USA. Since August 2021, BioInvent has a clinical trial collaboration and supply agreement with MSD, a tradename of Merck & Co., Inc., Rahway, NJ, USA, to evaluate the combination of BI-1808 and MSD's anti-PD-1 therapy KEYTRUDA (pembrolizumab).

About ovarian cancer
Ovarian cancer is a serious and life-threatening disease, affecting more than 320,000 women worldwide each year. 4 It is frequently diagnosed at an advanced stage because its symptoms are often difficult to recognize, and is the eighth most common cancer and the eighth leading cause of cancer-related death among women globally. 5 Recurrence affects an estimated 70-90% of patients with advanced disease after initial treatment. 6 Five-year survival rate is estimated at 50%, across all stages, types and regions. 7,8

About BI-1808
BI-1808 is a first-in-class drug candidate targeting TNFR2, which is upregulated on both immunosuppressive and inflammatory tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and on myeloid cells in the tumor microenvironment. BI-1808 is in clinical development for T-cell lymphoma and solid tumors, and has shown single-agent activity and excellent tolerability, and efficacy and a favorable safety profile in combination with pembrolizumab.

BI-1808 has received FDA Fast Track Designation for the treatment of ovarian cancer and for relapsed or refractory mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome, FDA Orphan Drug Designation for T-cell lymphoma, and Orphan Drug Designation in cutaneous T-cell lymphoma from the European Medicines Agency.

About BioInvent
BioInvent International AB (Nasdaq Stockholm:BINV) is a clinical-stage biotech company that discovers and develops novel and first-in-class immuno-modulatory antibodies for cancer therapy, with drug candidates in ongoing clinical programs in Phase 1/2 trials for the treatment of solid tumors and hematological cancer. The Company's validated, proprietary F.I.R.S.T™ technology platform identifies both targets and the antibodies that bind to them, generating many promising new immune-modulatory candidates to fuel the Company's own clinical development pipeline and providing licensing and partnering opportunities.

The Company generates revenues from research collaborations and license agreements with multiple top-tier pharmaceutical companies, as well as from producing antibodies for third parties in the Company's fully integrated manufacturing unit. More information is available at www.bioinvent.com.

data.title: Taiwan Brings Herbal Heritage and Modern Innovation to SupplySide Global 2026
data.description:
Taiwan Brings Herbal Heritage and Modern Innovation to SupplySide Global 2026

Taiwan Brings Herbal Heritage and Modern Innovation to SupplySide Global 2026

PR Newswire

LAS VEGAS, Oct. 24, 2026

LAS VEGAS, Oct. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- With a healthcare system that embraces both modern medicine and Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), Taiwan brings together herbal knowledge passed down over millennia, scientific evidence and modern pharmaceutical and biotechnology capabilities. Supported by the Department of Chinese Medicine and Pharmacy, Ministry of Health and Welfare, and organized by the Taiwan Institute of Economic Research, the Taiwan Traditional Chinese Medicine Pavilion will showcase four companies from the TCM and biotechnology sectors at SupplySide Global 2026 (Booth 7228), held October 28–30 in Las Vegas, translating this foundation into natural health ingredients, innovative wellness products and manufacturing partnerships for the global health and nutrition industry.

From Herbal Knowledge to Modern Wellness

Taiwan's healthcare ecosystem connects clinical practice, academic research and translational science, providing a foundation for its herbal industry. Drawing on traditional formulations and natural ingredient knowledge, companies combine research with modern dosage forms and delivery technologies to develop products for contemporary wellness needs. Quality management and flexible manufacturing support collaboration from ingredients to finished products.

Sun Ten Natureceutica adapts traditional herbal concepts into convenient wellness products supporting bone and joint health, women's wellness and restful sleep. Its portfolio includes jelly products, beverages and capsules, with food safety management certifications including FSSC 22000, ISO 22000 and HACCP.

Taiwan Three Mast Pharmaceutical combines herbal ingredients with topical delivery technologies, showcasing aromatherapy hot/cool patches and knee comfort patches. With Taiwan TCM GMP and Australian PIC/S GMP certifications, it offers customized patch development and OEM/ODM manufacturing.

Grape King Bio develops fermented mushroom ingredients from Antrodia cinnamomea, lion's mane and Cordyceps cicadae. FSSC 22000 and NSF GMP certifications support CDMO services from ingredient development to finished products.

Fu-Tian Pharmaceutical presents NRICM101, a Traditional Chinese medicine formulation indicated for "exogenous seasonal epidemic", alongside valerian extract capsules for relaxation and healthy sleep. With Taiwan TCM GMP certification, it offers OEM/ODM services spanning customized formulations, bulk herbal extracts and finished products.

Taiwan welcomes international partners to explore new possibilities in herbal wellness. By sharing its heritage, research and manufacturing expertise, the pavilion seeks to bring Taiwan's strengths to the world and contribute to healthier lives through long-term partnerships.

data.title: Likang Life Sciences Showcases Personalized Cancer Immunotherapy and Global Ambitions at Abu Dhabi Future Health Summit 2026
data.description:
Likang Life Sciences Showcases Personalized Cancer Immunotherapy and Global Ambitions at Abu Dhabi Future Health Summit 2026

Likang Life Sciences Showcases Personalized Cancer Immunotherapy and Global Ambitions at Abu Dhabi Future Health Summit 2026

PR Newswire

BEIJING, Oct. 24, 2026

BEIJING, Oct. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Likang Life Sciences ("Likang"), a biotechnology company advancing AI-enabled personalized cancer immunotherapies, sponsored and exhibited at the Abu Dhabi Future Health Summit 2026, held from 20 to 22 October at ADNEC Centre Abu Dhabi. The summit marked a milestone in Likang's international outreach, showcasing its scientific platform and clinical development programs.

Convened by the Department of Health – Abu Dhabi under the theme "To Sense Is to Predict," the event brought together leaders across healthcare, research and technology.

Likang Co-Founder and Vice Chairman Shannon Cheung joined a delegation of international health leaders received by UAE President His Highness Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan on 20 October. He also met Abu Dhabi Crown Prince His Highness Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan during his summit visit on 21 October. In brief exchanges, Cheung shared Likang's plans to bring its personalized cancer immunotherapy technologies and investigational therapies to Abu Dhabi, with a vision to develop the emirate as a platform for international research, innovation and future expansion.

Cheung spoke on "The Future of Cancer," moderated by Dr. Tarek Fadel of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), alongside Dr. Arie Belldegrun, Chairman of Bellco Health; Dr. Toni Choueiri of Harvard Medical School and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute; Prof. Dr. Angela George of The Royal Marsden; and Vinicius Ribeiro, CEO of Huna.

"The future of cancer care is not just about treating cancer earlier, but treating every patient more precisely, personally and effectively," Cheung said. He discussed how genomics, AI, mRNA technology and advanced cell manufacturing could support therapies tailored to individual tumor biology, while underscoring scalability and patient access.

At Booth AD28, Likang presented its AI-enabled neoantigen discovery platform and investigational immunotherapy pipeline. Its lead candidate, LK101, a personalized neoantigen mRNA-dendritic cell therapeutic cancer vaccine, received clinical trial authorization from China's National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) in 2023 and investigational new drug (IND) clearance from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 2025.

Building on ongoing dialogue with the Department of Health – Abu Dhabi and regional healthcare stakeholders, Likang is exploring opportunities in clinical research, AI-enabled precision oncology, scientific collaboration and potential future local manufacturing.

About Likang Life Sciences

Likang Life Sciences is a biotechnology company focused on AI-powered personalized cancer immunotherapy. Its pipeline includes personalized neoantigen therapeutic vaccines and neoantigen-specific T-cell therapies.

Website: www.likanglife.com
